outline_generation.overall_query: How do blue-collar workers in the U.S. perceive their jobs compared to other workers, based on recent survey data?
overall_checklist: How do blue-collar workers' job satisfaction levels compare to other workers?
What factors contribute to blue-collar workers' dissatisfaction with pay and work conditions?
How do blue-collar workers view their jobs in terms of career prospects, job-hunting, respect, and opportunities for education or training?

sections_summary.section_description: This section introduces the topic by highlighting the prominence of blue-collar workers in public discourse and outlines the scope and methodology of the Pew Research Center survey. It defines 'blue-collar workers' for the purposes of the analysis, describes the survey sample, and explains the rationale behind the sectoral and labor-based classification. Key sub-topics include: 1. Definition of blue-collar workers, 2. Survey methodology and sample characteristics.
sectional_checklist: Blue-collar workers are defined as those who do manual or physical labor in one of five industrial sectors: manufacturing, mining and construction; agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; retail and trade; hospitality or service; and transportation.
The survey was conducted among 5,273 employed U.S. adults, with 1,004 classified as blue-collar workers.

sections_summary.section_description: This section examines overall job satisfaction among blue-collar workers compared to other workers. It presents survey findings on satisfaction levels, with particular attention to age differences and satisfaction with pay. The section also discusses how blue-collar workers feel about various aspects of their work, including benefits and work hour flexibility, and highlights gender differences in pay satisfaction. Key sub-topics include: 1. Job satisfaction statistics, 2. Satisfaction with pay and benefits, 3. Gender and age differences.
sectional_checklist: 43% of blue-collar workers report being extremely or very satisfied with their jobs, compared to 53% of other workers.
Blue-collar workers are less satisfied with pay, benefits, and work hour flexibility than other workers; dissatisfaction with pay is especially common among women in blue-collar jobs.

sections_summary.section_description: This section explores how blue-collar workers perceive their jobs in terms of career prospects. It discusses the tendency for blue-collar workers to view their jobs as a means to get by rather than as careers, with breakdowns by gender and age. The section also notes the low percentage of workers who see their jobs as stepping stones to a career.
sectional_checklist: 54% of blue-collar workers describe their work as 'just a job to get you by,' compared to 27% of other workers.
Blue-collar women and younger blue-collar workers are especially likely to see their jobs as something just to get by, rather than as a career.

sections_summary.section_description: This section analyzes blue-collar workers' attitudes toward job-hunting and their optimism about finding new employment. It presents data on the likelihood of seeking a new job, differences by gender and age, and perceived ease or difficulty in finding desirable new positions.
sectional_checklist: 29% of blue-collar workers say it is very or somewhat likely they will look for a new job in the next six months, compared to 23% of other workers.
Blue-collar women and workers under 30 are more likely to consider job-hunting, but younger blue-collar workers are least optimistic about finding a job they want.

sections_summary.section_description: This section discusses how blue-collar workers feel about respect, both from society and within the workplace. It compares perceptions of societal respect between blue-collar and other workers, and details experiences of respect from supervisors, co-workers, and clients or customers. Gender differences in perceived respect are also addressed.
sectional_checklist: Only 31% of blue-collar workers feel most Americans have a great deal or fair amount of respect for their work, compared to 47% of other workers.
Most blue-collar workers report being treated respectfully by supervisors and co-workers, but these rates are still lower than among other workers.

sections_summary.section_description: This section covers blue-collar workers' views on education and training needed to advance at work. It details the proportion who feel they need more education or training, preferred methods for obtaining it, and differences in motivations for pursuing additional training between men and women. Key sub-topics include: 1. Perceived need for further education/training, 2. Preferred sources of training, 3. Gender differences in training motivations.
sectional_checklist: 31% of blue-collar workers say they need more education or training to get ahead at work, similar to other workers.
Few blue-collar workers see formal education as the best way to get needed training; on-the-job learning and certificate programs are preferred.

text_results.content:
The Center’s definition of blue-collar workers, who comprise about 27% of the U.S. workforce, includes people who do manual or physical labor in their jobs and work in one of five industry sectors:
* manufacturing, mining and construction
* agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting
* retail and trade
* hospitality or service
* transportation.

##  Blue-Collar Workers
The term blue-collar worker references individuals who engage in hard manual labor, typically in the agriculture, [manufacturing](), construction, mining, or maintenance sectors of the economy. Most of these people historically wore blue-collar shirts when they worked.

Our definition of “blue-collar workers” includes people who do manual or physical labor in their jobs _and_ work in one of five specific industrial sectors: manufacturing, mining and construction; agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; retail and trade; hospitality or service; and transportation.

How we did this
Pew Research Center conducted this study to better understand the experiences of American workers – specifically, blue-collar workers.
We surveyed 5,273 U.S. adults who are employed part or full time and either have one job  _or_ have more than one but consider one to be their primary job. The survey was conducted Oct. 7-13, 2024.

Over time, "blue-collar" became a broad label for anyone [engaged in manual labor]() or skilled trades, emphasizing the physical nature of their work compared to the office-based, intellectual tasks of their white-collar counterparts.

Historically, blue-collar workers have been the backbone of many industries, contributing directly to the production and maintenance of goods and infrastructure. These roles often involve working with machinery, tools, and various materials and can be found in settings such as factories, construction sites, and service industries.

## What is blue-collar work anyway?
While there’s no hard-and-fast definition, blue-collar work involves the production of goods, while white-collar work occurs at a desk in an office.
Although intuitive, the delineation between blue- and white-collar work leaves loads of room for interpretation, especially in today’s knowledge and service economy.

The term "blue-collar workers" originated in the early 20th century, reflecting the typical work attire of manual laborers. During the Industrial Revolution, many workers wore blue uniforms or work shirts, which were both durable and practical for the demanding conditions of factory and manual labor.

All of our findings are based on a survey conducted Oct. 7-13, 2024, among 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers we classified as blue-collar. (For more about the survey and how we defined blue-collar workers, read “How we did this.”)
_**Related:** [Most Americans Feel Good About Their Job Security but Not Their Pay]()_

Blue-collar workers were primarily involved in jobs requiring physical effort, such as [manufacturing](), construction, and maintenance, and their attire was designed to withstand the rigors of their tasks.

In October 2024, the Center surveyed 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers who were classified as blue-collar.
Key findings include:
* Blue-collar workers are markedly less satisfied with their jobs than other workers.

Wifi talents report that blue-collar workers make up about [13.4%]() of the total workforce in the United States. These individuals are engaged in manual labor or skilled trades, typically involving physical work. This category includes a diverse range of professions such as construction workers, electricians, plumbers, mechanics, and factory workers.

One of the most common ways to classify workers and jobs is by collar colors, with blue and white being the best known. Traditionally, [blue-collar]() jobs have involved manual labor, often in manufacturing or construction, and hourly or piecework pay. [White-collar]() jobs, on the other hand, are performed in offices, with work that is managerial, administrative, or clerical in nature. White collar workers are usually salaried.

For the purposes of this analysis, we defined “blue-collar workers” as those who do manual or physical labor in their jobs _and_ work in one of five specific industrial sectors: manufacturing, mining and construction; agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; retail and trade; hospitality and service; and transportation. In each of those sectors, more than 60% of workers do manual or physical labor in their jobs, and about 30% of workers or fewer have a bachelor’s degree. Together, those five sectors account for 39% of the U.S. workforce; those whose jobs involve manual/physical labor within those industries – who we term blue-collar workers – account for 27% of the workforce.

One way of conceptualizing occupational grades is the distinction between white-collar and blue-collar work. Blue-collar jobs are usually considered physically demanding, manual labour, which characterized much of the workforce during the industrial development of the labour market. White-collar work is typically defined as non-manual labour often in an office environment, e.g., managerial, professional, and service work (Herr et al., [Citation2015]()). However, the distinction between blue-collar and white-collar jobs has become more blurred today with the increase of skilled labour in modern western service society (Alvesson, [Citation2004]()). Consequently, the white-collar and the blue-collar groups have expanded to include both low-skilled and high-skilled jobs (see e.g., Lau, [Citation2008]()). In the public sector, for example, the low-skilled white-collar group typically consists of employees who perform non-supervisory clerical tasks or low-skilled service tasks primarily related to health and child care (Della Torre et al., [Citation2015]()). Studies have shown that low-skilled and high-skilled white-collar employees may differ in their perceptions of and attitudes to sickness absence (Wynne-Jones et al., [Citation2011]()).

* Blue-collar jobs usually involve manual labor, and workers are paid on an hourly or piecework basis.
* Certain perceptions aren't necessarily accurate, including those that hold that blue-collar workers belong to a lower social class and that white-collar jobs pay more.

Some blue-collar workers may have to do physically demanding or exhausting tasks. They may work outdoors and/or with heavy machinery or animals. Workers may be [skilled]() or [unskilled](). Skills can be acquired on the job or, more commonly, at a trade school.
Some of the most common blue-collar jobs include:
* Welders
* Mechanics
* Electricians

## Who are blue collar workers?
![Three blue paper boats]()Who are blue collar workers?

Pew Research Center has a history of studying digital technology adoption. For the new material in this report, the Center surveyed 1,502 U.S. adults from Jan. 25 to Feb. 8, 2021, by cellphone and landline phone. The survey was conducted by interviewers under the direction of Abt Associates and is weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, education and other categories. Here are [the questions used]() for this report, along with responses, and its methodology.

"The Blue-Collar Drought" refers to the growing shortage of skilled blue-collar workers in various industries. This term [highlights the challenges]() faced by employers in filling positions that require technical skills and manual labor, which are essential for maintaining and expanding industrial and infrastructural capabilities.

A particularly robust finding from studies comparing job satisfaction across these groups is that blue-collar workers tend to be less satisfied than their white-collar counterparts with various aspects of their jobs, such as pay (e.g., Lee et al., 1981, Weaver, 1975), their supervisors (e.g., O’farrell and Harlan, 1982), and the work itself (e.g., Lee et al., 1981, O’farrell and Harlan, 1982).

Some fascinating takeaways in this new analysis of blue collar workers from my colleagues [Luona Lin]() and [Drew DeSilver](). Compared with other workers, blue collar workers are less satisfied with their jobs overall, feel less respected by the public, are less attached to their jobs, and are more likely to view their jobs as just a way to get them by, rather than as a career. Other interesting insights: ➡️ One of the biggest gaps between blue collar workers and other workers in terms of job satisfaction is in how they feel about the amount of flexibility they have to work remotely. Only 20% of blue collar workers are satisfied with this aspect of their job vs. 43% of other workers. ➡️ Women in blue collar jobs are much less likely than men to say they think of their job as a career rather than just a job to get them by (24% of women vs. 39%). Blue collar women are also more likely than men to say most people in the U.S. don't have respect for the type of work they do (41% of women vs. 31% of men). ➡️ Older blue collar workers are more satisfied with their jobs overall than younger blue collar workers. They're also more likely to view their job as a career (48% among blue collar workers ages 50 and older vs. 15% among those younger than 30).

Among blue-collar workers, 43% say they feel extremely or very satisfied with their jobs; by comparison, 53% of other workers express this level of satisfaction. And 15% of blue-collar workers are not too or not at all satisfied, compared with 10% of other workers.

Blue-collar workers are markedly less satisfied with their jobs than other workers. They feel less respected, are less attached to their jobs, and are more likely to view their jobs as just a way to get by, rather than as a career. Younger blue-collar workers and women in blue-collar jobs are especially likely to hold these views.

# Blue-collar workers are less satisfied at work, less attached to their jobs than other U.S. workers
By [Drew DeSilver]() and [Luona Lin]()

### Blue‑collar vs. other workers
Only **43% of blue‑collar workers** say they’re highly satisfied, compared to **53% among other occupations**.
Older blue‑collar workers (50+) fare better, with **56% highly satisfied** , while younger ones lag significantly in satisfaction and pay perceptions.
Source: [Pew Research]()

Beyond pay, blue-collar workers are less satisfied than other workers with various other aspects of their work lives, from their health insurance and other benefits to the flexibility of their work hours. One exception: Among workers who commute to their jobs, about equal shares of blue-collar and other workers (59% and 57%) are extremely or very satisfied with their commutes.

* Among all blue-collar workers, just a quarter say they’re extremely or very satisfied with how much they’re paid, while a third are not too or not at all satisfied. Among other workers, 32% are extremely or very satisfied with their pay, while 28% are not too or not at all satisfied. Dissatisfaction with pay is particularly common among women in blue-collar jobs: 40% say they’re not too or not at all satisfied with their pay, compared with 30% of men in these jobs.

However, slightly more than half of blue-collar workers ages 50 and older (56%) say they’re extremely or very satisfied with their jobs – considerably higher than the share among younger blue-collar workers. In particular, 32% of older blue-collar workers are extremely or very satisfied with their pay, while younger blue-collar workers are less likely to feel this way.

Across different age groups, the oldest blue-collar workers are most likely to view their jobs as careers: About half of those ages 50 and older (48%) see their jobs this way. Conversely, 65% of blue-collar workers ages 18 to 29 view their jobs as just something they do to get by.

Studies have emphasized the higher quality of employment and better work conditions in white-collar occupations (Fagan & Burchell, [2002]( "Fagan, C., & Burchell, B. \(2002\). Gender, jobs and working conditions in the European union. Office of the Official Publication of the European Communities.")). Workers in high-level white-collar occupations enjoy more training opportunities than blue-collar workers (Diekhoff et al., [2007]( "Diekhoff, M., Jungblut, J-M., & O’Connell, P. J. \(2007\). Job related training in europe: Do institutions matter? In D. Gallie \(Ed.\), Employment regimes and the quality of work \(pp. 77–104\). Oxford University Press.")); Fagan & Burchell, [2002]( "Fagan, C., & Burchell, B. \(2002\). Gender, jobs and working conditions in the European union. Office of the Official Publication of the European Communities."); Tahlin, [2007]( "Tahlin, M. \(2007\). Skills and wages in European labour markets: Structure and change. In D. Gallie \(Ed.\), Employment regimes and the quality of work \(pp. 35–76\). Oxford University Press.")), and highly skilled workers have better monetary as well as non-monetary rewards compared to low skilled workers (Stier, [2015]( "Stier, H. \(2015\). The skill-divide in job quality: A cross-national analysis. Social Science Research, 49, 70–80.")). Studies show these benefits are gendered, as men tend to be in better quality jobs than women, with more extrinsic and intrinsic benefits (Stier & Yaish, [2014]( "Stier, H., & Yaish, M. \(2014\). Occupational segregation and gender inequality in job quality: A multi-level approach. Work Employment & Society, 28\(2\), 225–246.")). In the current study we distinguish high status PTM (professional, technical and managerial) jobs from low white-collar and blue-collar jobs because high status PTM jobs are likely to be “good” jobs that offer higher income and more intrinsic benefits than other jobs. Furthermore, we also interact PTM employment with full-part time, to test which aspect of employment contributes more to well-being.

Dissatisfaction with pay is particularly common among women in blue-collar jobs: 40% say they’re not too or not at all satisfied with their pay, compared with 30% of men in these jobs.

To say one person works a blue-collar job while another has a white-collar job implies a [difference in earnings](). The blue-collar worker may work for [hourly wages]() or receive payment per item produced or assembled. They may be part of a union that maintains the security of hours and future work.

* Blue-collar workers are markedly less satisfied with their jobs than other workers.

When it comes to who experiences higher levels of stress—white- or blue-collar workers—the research is inconclusive. Some studies have found that blue-collar workers had a [1.5 times higher]() risk of stress compared to their white-collar counterparts and had a higher tendency to smoke or be overweight or obese; whereas other studies conclude that the white-collar industry endures the largest amount of stress due to workers’ sedentary behavior and high decision latitude, which results in the same outcomes.2

However, slightly more than half of blue-collar workers ages 50 and older (56%) say they’re extremely or very satisfied with their jobs – considerably higher than the share among younger blue-collar workers. All of our findings are based on a survey conducted Oct. 7-13, 2024, among 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers we classified as blue-collar. (For more about the survey and how we defined blue-collar workers, read “How we did this.”)
_**Related:** [Most Americans Feel Good About Their Job Security but Not Their Pay]()_

In October 2024, the Center surveyed 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers who were classified as blue-collar.
Key findings include:
* Blue-collar workers are markedly less satisfied with their jobs than other workers.

* Blue-collar workers are a bit more likely than other workers to say they expect to look for a new job soon, though they have doubts about finding a position they’ll like. Blue-collar men are a bit more optimistic in this regard than blue-collar women. And the youngest blue-collar workers – those under 30 – are the least optimistic about finding a new job they’d want.

For this paper, we follow others in defining blue-collar workers as those who perform primarily physical work and whose career paths are relatively restricted (Gibson and Papa, 2000, Lederer, 1987) and white-collar workers as professional and semi-professional employees (Hammer & Ferrari, 2002). A particularly robust finding from studies comparing job satisfaction across these groups is that blue-collar workers tend to be less satisfied than their white-collar counterparts with various aspects of their jobs, such as pay (e.g., Lee et al., 1981, Weaver, 1975), their supervisors (e.g., O’farrell and Harlan, 1982), and the work itself (e.g., Lee et al., 1981, O’farrell and Harlan, 1982).
Blue-collar women (33%) and those ages 18 to 29 (44%) are among the subgroups most likely to say they’re very or somewhat likely to look for a new job soon.

After taking center stage throughout the bulk of the media’s coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic, blue-collar workers say they’ve gained more respect and appreciation from the people they serve—and have gained a newfound sense of appreciation for their own work as a result. According to recent findings from the Harris Poll, roughly nine in 10 blue-collar workers [feel proud]() of the work that they do, a feeling that more than a third attribute to their ability to help others and perform purposeful and meaningful work.

According to recent findings from the Harris Poll, roughly nine in 10 blue-collar workers [feel proud]() of the work that they do, a feeling that more than a third attribute to their ability to help others and perform purposeful and meaningful work.

Only around three-in-ten blue-collar workers (31%) say most Americans have a great deal or a fair amount of respect for the work they do, compared with nearly half of other workers (47%). Conversely, 35% of blue-collar workers (including 41% of women) say most Americans don’t respect their work much or at all – a sentiment shared by just 19% of other workers.

All of our findings are based on a survey conducted Oct. 7-13, 2024, among 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers we classified as blue-collar. (For more about the survey and how we defined blue-collar workers, read “How we did this.”)
_**Related:** [Most Americans Feel Good About Their Job Security but Not Their Pay]()_

Attitudes are somewhat more positive when it comes to being respected on the job. Most of blue-collar workers (78%) say their supervisor treats them respectfully all or most of the time, though that’s still fewer than the 83% of other workers who say the same. Most blue-collar workers and other workers (83% and 87%) say their co-workers treat them with respect all or most of the time.

Job pride, especially among blue-collar workers, remains an understudied subject, even though other positive aspects of work, such as work engagement ([Bakker and Albrecht, 2018](javascript:;); [Knight _et al._ , 2017](javascript:;)), meaningful work ([Carton, 2018](javascript:;); [Lips-Wiersma _et al._ , 2016](javascript:;)), dignity ([Buzzanell and Lucas, 2013](javascript:;); [Lucas, 2011](javascript:;); [Lucas and Buzzanell, 2004](javascript:;)) and recognition ([Arnolds _et al._ , 2010](javascript:;)), have received significantly more attention. Blue-collar work is seen as dirty, physically demanding, low-skilled and low-paid activity, providing little or no intrinsic value for workers ([Torlina, 2011](javascript:;)). It is not typically seen as a source of pride, unlike professional jobs. This was the dominant view of industrial sociologists ([Springer, 1999](javascript:;)) until the turn of the millennium, when positive psychology began to gain ground. More recent accounts have pointed out that blue-collar workers may find their work important, meaningful and something to be proud of after all ([Lips-Wiersma _et al._ , 2016](javascript:;); [Kreiner _et al._ , 2006](javascript:;); [Torlina, 2011](javascript:;)).

Meanwhile, among blue-collar workers who interact with customers or clients, two-thirds (67%) say they’re treated with respect in those relationships all or most of the time, compared with about three-quarters of other workers (74%).
(These figures exclude workers who say they don’t have co-workers, supervisors, or clients or customers.)

In October 2024, the Center surveyed 5,273 employed U.S. adults, including 1,004 workers who were classified as blue-collar.
Key findings include:
* Blue-collar workers are markedly less satisfied with their jobs than other workers.

Some fascinating takeaways in this new analysis of blue collar workers from my colleagues [Luona Lin]() and [Drew DeSilver](). Compared with other workers, blue collar workers are less satisfied with their jobs overall, feel less respected by the public, are less attached to their jobs, and are more likely to view their jobs as just a way to get them by, rather than as a career. Other interesting insights: ➡️ One of the biggest gaps between blue collar workers and other workers in terms of job satisfaction is in how they feel about the amount of flexibility they have to work remotely. Only 20% of blue collar workers are satisfied with this aspect of their job vs. 43% of other workers. ➡️ Women in blue collar jobs are much less likely than men to say they think of their job as a career rather than just a job to get them by (24% of women vs. 39%). Blue collar women are also more likely than men to say most people in the U.S. don't have respect for the type of work they do (41% of women vs. 31% of men). ➡️ Older blue collar workers are more satisfied with their jobs overall than younger blue collar workers. They're also more likely to view their job as a career (48% among blue collar workers ages 50 and older vs. 15% among those younger than 30).

How we did this
Pew Research Center conducted this study to better understand the experiences of American workers – specifically, blue-collar workers.
We surveyed 5,273 U.S. adults who are employed part or full time and either have one job  _or_ have more than one but consider one to be their primary job. The survey was conducted Oct. 7-13, 2024.

Meanwhile, among blue-collar workers who interact with customers or clients, two-thirds (67%) say they’re treated with respect in those relationships all or most of the time, compared with about three-quarters of other workers (74%).
(These figures exclude workers who say they don’t have co-workers, supervisors, or clients or customers.)

Attitudes are somewhat more positive when it comes to being respected on the job. Most of blue-collar workers (78%) say their supervisor treats them respectfully all or most of the time, though that’s still fewer than the 83% of other workers who say the same. Most blue-collar workers and other workers (83% and 87%) say their co-workers treat them with respect all or most of the time.

Despite the analysis lending support to the interpretation that blue-collar workers are active individuals who have healthy self-worth, manual labour commands far less respect outside the confines of factories and working-class communities. To borrow [Goodheart's (2020)](javascript:;) distinction, society at large, and the mainstream media in particular, glorify people who work with their _heads_ (cognitive work) and dismiss those who work either with their _hands_ (manual work) or _hearts_ (care work). This article offers no panacea to this problem, but it would certainly be beneficial if blue-collar work received more scholarly attention than it currently does.

### **Overview**
In March 2025, the Pew Research Center issued findings from its recent research on blue-collar workers, as reported in “[Blue-collar workers are less satisfied at work, less attached to their jobs than other U.S. workers]().”

Some fascinating takeaways in this new analysis of blue collar workers from my colleagues [Luona Lin]() and [Drew DeSilver](). Among blue-collar workers who say they need more education or training to get ahead, only 17% say formal education – for example, a high school diploma or college degree – would be the best way to get it, compared with 27% of other workers. Some 63% of adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher level of education say they will need to keep advancing their skills throughout their career, compared with 45% of those with no college experience who feel the same sense of urgency. Government data reinforce this finding as workers with higher levels of education are more likely to engage in job training or acquire job certificates or licenses.

For the purposes of this analysis, we defined “blue-collar workers” as those who do manual or physical labor in their jobs _and_ work in one of five specific industrial sectors: manufacturing, mining and construction; agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; retail and trade; hospitality and service; and transportation.
